chapter: Piano craft and the New York school
title: New York stride school versus Western blues, and show business influence
summary: Ramirez argues New York's show-business melody mixed with the Blues, citing James P. Johnson and Gershwin.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Now, Jelly Roll's thing... It seems to me that the New York School (from listening to records) was based primarily on the stride thing.
Well, that was in vogue in the Twenties, you see.
That was Fats, that was James P., it was Duke, it was Donald Lambert, Willie The Loin Smith...
See, now, the unknowns... At the time that you're speaking about, the ones that had more exposure than
Ramirez - 170
the others. Like Duke or Fats, they had more exposure than the other runner-ups. You know what I mean? But it was the same style.
What I was really getting at was that when Jelly Roll Morton and Earl came to New York, they were sort of Western.
Blues, yeah.
Well, Jonah Jones told me that they all thought that anything from Chicago was Western in New York.

But you must remember that it was Blues-oriented, the ones from the West. When you came to New York, you had the atmosphere of Broadway, Show Business, Pop Music, Tin Pan Alley, and you had ethnical...the ethnic groups or other groups were much more together, much more mixed than they were outside of New York. You know what I mean?
Yes.
There's a lot of people on Manhattan Island. But that's only an island. You see? And therefore, the melody of show business creeps into the Blues...
Dominates it.
Dominates it, see.
That's very good.
Yeah, maybe, because in some of J.P.'s...
No, I mean that's a good point.
Ramirez - 171

Some of J.P.'s accompaniment to singers I heard on the old-fashioned records, he would play something out of Gershwin)'s music, "Rhapsody In Blue" or something like that. But in his touch of blues, you hardly noticed it. But if you're familiar with the composition of "Rhapsody in Blue" or some of the parts of this... And Gershwin was vice-versa, too. He would do a lot of Johnson's... "A Woman Is A Sometime Thing", the opening of Porgy and Bess, I mean to me it's all Johnson with, of course, extra harmony added. But I mean, Gershwin was such an innovator. I mean, you just can't underplay his Rhapsody on the Blues, you know.

I think you're making a very good point here. Because Chicago being spread out more, the thing wouldn't be integrated in the same way as it would in New York. Black and White were compelled to mingle by the island.
